source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 20 (PDF 59-74, printed 56-71); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 20 (Aromatic Hydrocarbons), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 The molecular formula of benzene is:
blocks.explanation: Benzene is an important organic compound with the chemical formula C₆H₆ (20.1).

book_ref.quote: Benzene is one of the most important organic compounds with the chemical formula C₆H₆.

blocks.prompt: 2 The simplest aromatic hydrocarbon is:
blocks.explanation: Benzene, C₆H₆, is the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon (20.1). Cyclohexane has no benzene ring; phenol is not a hydrocarbon.

book_ref.quote: It is the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon.

blocks.prompt: 3 Arenes are organic hydrocarbons that contain:

options.text: only single bonds in an open chain
a cyclic ring of sp³ carbons only

blocks.explanation: Organic hydrocarbons containing one or more benzene rings are known as arenes (20.1).

book_ref.quote: Organic hydrocarbons containing one or more benzene rings are known as arenes.

blocks.prompt: 4 In the early 19th century, compounds containing benzene rings were called 'aromatic' because they were:
blocks.explanation: Benzene-derived products are pleasantly fragrant, so such compounds were classified as 'aromatic' (sweet smelling) (20.1).

book_ref.quote: Benzene derived products are well known to be pleasantly fragrant.

blocks.prompt: 5 Today the term 'aromatic' is used for molecules that:

options.text: have benzene or benzene-like rings, even if they smell foul
contain any ring of carbon atoms
contain at least one double bond

blocks.explanation: The term 'aromatic' now designates molecules with benzene and benzene-like rings, including ones that have foul smells (20.1).

book_ref.quote: that are not good-smelling, rather have foul smells

blocks.prompt: 6 Camphor has a strong minty aroma. This shows that:

options.text: a pleasant smell does not prove a compound is aromatic

blocks.explanation: Camphor, from the camphor laurel tree, has a strong minty aroma but lacks a benzene ring; so smell alone does not make a compound aromatic (20.1, Did You Know?).

book_ref.quote: Non-aromatic compounds, such as camphor, extracted from the camphor laurel tree

blocks.prompt: 7 Which of the following is given as a sweet-smelling aromatic compound?
blocks.explanation: Many aromatic compounds are pleasant smelling, such as vanilla (20.1). Camphor smells strongly but is non-aromatic.

book_ref.quote: Many aromatic compounds are sweet/pleasant smelling, such as vanilla.

blocks.prompt: 8 The linear structures first proposed for benzene were rejected because they:

options.text: could not explain the properties of benzene

blocks.explanation: Some scientists presented linear structures for C₆H₆, but these could not explain the properties of benzene and were soon rejected (20.1).

book_ref.quote: But, these were soon rejected as they could not explain the properties of benzene.

blocks.prompt: 9 August Kekule proposed the structure of benzene in:
blocks.explanation: The structure of benzene remained a mystery until 1865, when the German professor August Kekule elucidated it (20.1).

book_ref.quote: until 1865 when a German professor August Kekule elucidated it

blocks.prompt: 10 According to Kekule, benzene is a:

options.text: six-membered ring with alternate single and double bonds
six-membered ring with only single bonds
straight chain with two triple bonds
five-membered ring with one double bond

blocks.explanation: Kekule described benzene as a six-membered cyclic compound having alternate single and double bonds (20.1).

book_ref.quote: six membered cyclic compound having alternate single and double bonds

blocks.prompt: 11 X-ray studies show that the benzene molecule is:
blocks.explanation: X-ray studies show a planar configuration: a regular hexagon of six sp² hybridized carbon atoms (20.1).

book_ref.quote: planar configuration characterized by a regular hexagon

blocks.prompt: 12 The C–C–C and H–C–C bond angles in benzene are:
blocks.explanation: Each carbon is connected to three atoms with bond angles of 120° for C–C–C and H–C–C (20.1).

book_ref.quote: bond angles of 120° for C–C–C and H–C–C

blocks.prompt: 13 The carbon-carbon bond length in benzene is:
blocks.explanation: All C–C bonds in benzene are 139 pm, between the C–C single bond (154 pm) and the C=C double bond (133 pm) (20.1, Table 20.1).

book_ref.quote: while the length of the C–C bond is 139 pm

blocks.prompt: 14 The C–H bond length in benzene is:
blocks.explanation: The length of the C–H bond in benzene is 109 pm (1.090 Å) (20.1).

book_ref.quote: The length of the C–H bond is 109 pm

blocks.prompt: 15 The C–C bond length of benzene is 1.3970 Å. Since 1 Å = 100 pm, this equals:
blocks.explanation: 1.3970 Å × 100 pm/Å = 139.7 pm, which the chapter rounds to 139 pm (20.1).

book_ref.quote: All C-C and C-H bond lengths are 1.3970 Å and 1.090 Å, respectively.

blocks.prompt: 16 The main problem with Kekule's structure was that it:

options.text: did not fully explain the physical and chemical properties of benzene
did not show six carbon atoms
showed benzene as a straight chain

blocks.explanation: Kekule's structure explained many properties but did not fully explain the physical and chemical properties of benzene (20.1).

book_ref.quote: it didn’t fully explain the physical and chemical properties of benzene

blocks.text: 20.1.1 Thermodynamic Stability of Benzene and Resonance

blocks.prompt: 17 The heat released when cyclohexene is hydrogenated to cyclohexane is:
blocks.explanation: Hydrogenation of cyclohexene (one C=C) gives cyclohexane and releases 120 kJ mol⁻¹ (20.1.1).

book_ref.quote: The hydrogenation of cyclohexene results in the formation of cyclohexane and releases 120 kJ mol⁻¹ of energy.

blocks.prompt: 18 The expected heat of complete hydrogenation of cyclohexadiene is:
blocks.explanation: Two C=C bonds × 120 kJ mol⁻¹ = 240 kJ mol⁻¹ (20.1.1).

book_ref.quote: we could expect that cyclohexadiene would yield 240 kJ mol⁻¹ on complete hydrogenation

blocks.prompt: 19 The heat of hydrogenation expected for the hypothetical 1,3,5-cyclohexatriene is:
blocks.explanation: Three C=C bonds × 120 kJ mol⁻¹ = 360 kJ mol⁻¹ (20.1.1).

book_ref.quote: the hypothetical 1,3,5-cyclohexatriene would produce 360 kJ mol⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 20 The actual heat of hydrogenation of benzene is:
blocks.explanation: Benzene releases only 208 kJ mol⁻¹ on hydrogenation, much lower than 360 kJ mol⁻¹, showing exceptional stability (20.1.1).

book_ref.quote: Benzene, however, has much lower heat of hydrogenation (208 kJ mol⁻¹) exhibiting an exceptional stability.

blocks.prompt: 21 The resonance energy of benzene is:
blocks.explanation: Resonance energy = 360 − 208 = 152 kJ mol⁻¹ (20.1.1; the printed 158.5 is a misprint, see the Book correction).

book_ref.quote: The actual heat of hydrogenation of benzene is 152 kJ mol⁻¹ lower than the theoretical value.

blocks.prompt: 22 Resonance energy of benzene is also called:
blocks.explanation: The energy by which benzene's actual heat of hydrogenation is lower than the theoretical value is the resonance energy (delocalisation energy) (20.1.1).

book_ref.quote: This energy is called the resonance energy (delocalisation energy) of benzene.

blocks.prompt: 23 Cyclohexene, cyclohexadiene and benzene all give which common product on complete catalytic hydrogenation?
blocks.explanation: Catalytic addition of hydrogen to all of them yields cyclohexane, the common product and low-energy reference point (20.1.1).

book_ref.quote: This reaction yields cyclohexane as a common product via catalytic addition of hydrogen.

blocks.prompt: 24 In the energy level diagram of hydrogenation (Figure 20.1), cyclohexane represents:
blocks.explanation: Cyclohexane is the common product, so it symbolizes a low-energy reference point against which the other compounds are compared (20.1.1).

book_ref.quote: cyclohexane symbolizes a low-energy reference point

blocks.prompt: 25 A lower heat of hydrogenation than expected shows that the compound is:
blocks.explanation: Heats of hydrogenation relate to thermodynamic stability; benzene's low value (208 instead of 360 kJ mol⁻¹) shows it is much more stable (20.1.1).

book_ref.quote: These heats of hydrogenation can be related to the relative thermodynamic stability of the compounds.

blocks.prompt: 26 A cyclic alkene with one C=C releases 118 kJ mol⁻¹ on hydrogenation. An aromatic ring analogue with three such bonds releases only 205 kJ mol⁻¹. Its resonance energy is:
blocks.explanation: Expected = 3 × 118 = 354 kJ mol⁻¹; resonance energy = 354 − 205 = 149 kJ mol⁻¹ (method of 20.1.1).

book_ref.quote: Evidence of the increased stability of benzene is obtained by measuring the heat emitted

blocks.prompt: 27 The extra stability of benzene is explained by:

options.text: the presence of only σ bonds
delocalisation of π electrons over the ring

blocks.explanation: The stability is explained by delocalisation of π electrons over all six carbon atoms through π orbital overlap (20.1.1).

book_ref.quote: This stability is explained based on the delocalisation of π electrons.

blocks.prompt: 28 The hybridization of each carbon atom in benzene is:
blocks.explanation: According to the hybridization approach each carbon atom in benzene is sp² hybridized (20.1.2).

book_ref.quote: each carbon atom in benzene is sp² hybridized

blocks.prompt: 29 Each carbon atom of benzene forms how many σ bonds?
blocks.explanation: The three sp² orbitals of each carbon form three σ bonds: two with adjacent carbons and one with hydrogen (20.1.2).

book_ref.quote: two with adjacent carbon atoms and one with a hydrogen atom

blocks.prompt: 30 The total number of σ bonds in one benzene molecule is:
blocks.explanation: Six C–C σ bonds in the ring and six C–H σ bonds: 6 + 6 = 12 (20.1.2).

book_ref.quote: The three sp² hybrid orbitals on each carbon are utilized to form three σ-bonds

blocks.prompt: 31 The six unhybridized 2p orbitals in benzene are:

options.text: in the plane of the ring
perpendicular to the σ framework and parallel to each other

blocks.explanation: One unhybridized 2p orbital per carbon lies perpendicular to the σ framework, parallel to the others, so they overlap sideways (20.1.2).

book_ref.quote: are perpendicular to this sigma framework and parallel to each other

blocks.prompt: 32 In benzene the π-electron cloud lies:

options.text: only in the plane of the ring
only between C and H atoms
outside the ring along C–H bonds
above and below the plane of the ring

blocks.explanation: Sideways overlap of the 2p orbitals forms a π-electron cloud above and below the plane of the ring (20.1.2).

book_ref.quote: form a π-electron cloud above and below the plane of the benzene ring

blocks.prompt: 33 How many π electrons are delocalized over the benzene ring?
blocks.explanation: Due to the overlap six π electrons are shared equally among all six carbons: delocalization of π electrons (20.1.2).

book_ref.quote: six electrons are shared equally among all the six carbons

blocks.prompt: 34 In the hexagon-with-circle symbol of benzene, the circle stands for:
blocks.explanation: Benzene is represented as a hexagon with an inscribed circle; the circle represents the delocalized π electrons (20.1.2).

book_ref.quote: where the circle represents delocalized π electrons

blocks.prompt: 35 All six C–C bond lengths in benzene are equal because of:
blocks.explanation: Delocalization makes all six C–C bond lengths the same (139 pm); alternate single and double bonds would give two lengths (20.1.2).

book_ref.quote: This delocalization causes all the six C - C bond lengths to be same (139 pm).

blocks.prompt: 36 According to Table 20.1, the C≡C bond length is:
blocks.explanation: Table 20.1 gives C–C 154 pm, C=C 133 pm and C≡C 120 pm (20.1.2).

book_ref.quote: making it a conjugated molecule

blocks.prompt: 37 The C–H σ bond in benzene is formed by the overlap of:

options.text: sp² orbital of C and sp² orbital of H
sp² orbital of C and 1s orbital of H
2p orbital of C and 1s orbital of H
sp³ orbital of C and 1s orbital of H

blocks.explanation: Hydrogen bonds with its 1s orbital, so the C–H bond is sp²–s (20.1.2, Book correction to the printed 'sp2-sp2').

book_ref.quote: hydrogen bonds with its 1s orbital, so the bond is sp2-s

blocks.prompt: 38 All carbon and hydrogen atoms of the benzene σ framework lie in one plane because:

options.text: the 2p orbitals are in the plane
hydrogen atoms repel the π cloud
all the sp² orbitals are in the same plane

blocks.explanation: Since all sp² orbitals lie in the same plane, the σ framework atoms are coplanar at 120° (20.1.2).

book_ref.quote: all the carbon and hydrogen atoms of this σ framework are coplanar at 120°

blocks.prompt: 39 Aromatic hydrocarbons containing only one benzene ring are called:
blocks.explanation: Aromatic hydrocarbons with only one benzene ring are monocyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (20.2).

book_ref.quote: are known as monocyclic aromatic hydrocarbons

blocks.prompt: 40 Aromatic hydrocarbons with two or more benzene rings are called:
blocks.explanation: Aromatic hydrocarbons with two or more benzene rings are polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (20.2).

book_ref.quote: two or more benzene rings in their molecules are known as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons

blocks.prompt: 41 Benzene derivatives are named in:

options.text: one style only: with the suffix 'benzene'
three styles: Greek, Latin and IUPAC
two styles: with the suffix 'benzene' or with a special name

blocks.explanation: There are two styles: naming with the suffix 'benzene' (e.g. nitrobenzene) and special names without 'benzene' (e.g. phenol) (20.2).

book_ref.quote: There are two styles of naming benzene derivatives.

blocks.prompt: 42 C₆H₅NO₂ is named, with benzene as the base name:
blocks.explanation: Monosubstituted benzenes are named with the base name 'benzene' and the substituent as prefix: nitrobenzene (20.2).

book_ref.quote: such as chlorobenzene, nitrobenzene and methyl benzene

blocks.prompt: 43 The IUPAC-accepted common base name for C₆H₅CH₃ is:
blocks.explanation: Some common names are IUPAC base names: phenol (C₆H₅OH), toluene (C₆H₅CH₃), aniline (C₆H₅NH₂) (20.2).

book_ref.quote: e.g, phenol, toluene, aniline, etc.

blocks.prompt: 44 The IUPAC-accepted base name of C₆H₅NH₂ is:
blocks.explanation: Aniline is a common name included in IUPAC nomenclature as the base name for C₆H₅NH₂ (20.2).

book_ref.quote: some of these names have been included in IUPAC nomenclature as base names for the structure

blocks.prompt: 45 No locant number is written in the name of a monosubstituted benzene because:

options.text: the substituent is always at C-1

blocks.explanation: In a monosubstituted benzene the substituent is always at C-1, so there is no need to number it (20.2).

book_ref.quote: The substituent in a monosubstituted benzene is always at C-1, so there is no need to number its location.

blocks.prompt: 46 Which substituent has the highest priority for numbering a disubstituted benzene?
blocks.explanation: The priority order is –COOH > –CN > –CHO > –COCH₃ > –OH > –NH₂ > –OR > –R (20.2).

book_ref.quote: The order of priority of substituents (left to right) is

blocks.prompt: 47 A benzene ring carries –OH and –NH₂ on carbons that are meta to each other. Its name is:
blocks.explanation: –OH has higher priority than –NH₂, so its carbon is C₁ (base name phenol); the meta carbon is C₃: 3-aminophenol (20.2).

book_ref.quote: The carbon to which a higher priority substituent is attached is C₁.

blocks.prompt: 48 A benzene ring has a bromine and a chlorine atom in 1,3 positions. Its correct name is:
blocks.explanation: With equal priority, the substituent earlier in the alphabet (bromo before chloro) gets C₁: 1-bromo-3-chlorobenzene (20.2).

book_ref.quote: If both substituents are the same priority then the carbon having a substituent lower in alphabets is designated as C₁.

blocks.prompt: 49 A benzene ring carries –COOH and –NO₂ on opposite (1,4) carbons. Its name is:
blocks.explanation: –COOH has top priority, so it fixes C₁ (benzoic acid); –NO₂ on the opposite carbon is at C₄: 4-nitrobenzoic acid (20.2).

book_ref.quote: Common names in bold face given below are considered to be IUPAC correct base names for structures.

blocks.prompt: 50 Two substituents at positions 1 and 2 of a benzene ring are described as:
blocks.explanation: Ortho (o-) = 1,2; meta (m-) = 1,3; para (p-) = 1,4 (20.2, Did You Know?).

book_ref.quote: ortho- (o-), meta- (m-), or para (p-) can be used in place of positional markers

blocks.prompt: 51 Two substituents at positions 1 and 3 of a benzene ring are described as:
blocks.explanation: Positions 1 and 3 are meta (m-) to each other (20.2).

book_ref.quote: Disubstituted benzenes have common names with reference to the relationship between the two substituents.

blocks.prompt: 52 1,4-Dibromobenzene is also called:
blocks.explanation: Bromine atoms at positions 1 and 4 are para: p-dibromobenzene (20.2, Book correction to the printed 'ortho (1,3)').

book_ref.quote: bromine atoms at positions 1 and 4 are para (1,4)

blocks.text: 20.3 Comparison of Reactivity of Benzene with Alkanes and Alkenes

blocks.prompt: 53 Alkanes are generally unreactive because they:

options.text: are non-polar and have only σ bonds

blocks.explanation: Alkanes are unreactive due to their non-polar nature and presence of σ bonds only (20.3).

book_ref.quote: Alkanes are generally an unreactive class of organic compounds due to their non-polar nature and the presence of sigma bond only.

blocks.prompt: 54 In the presence of UV light, alkanes readily undergo:
blocks.explanation: Alkanes undergo free radical substitution reactions quite easily in the presence of UV light (20.3).

book_ref.quote: they undergo free radical substitution reactions in the presence of UV light quite easily

blocks.prompt: 55 Alkenes are very reactive and typically undergo:
blocks.explanation: Because of the π bond and available π electrons, alkenes undergo electrophilic addition easily (20.3).

book_ref.quote: They undergo electrophilic addition reactions easily.

blocks.prompt: 56 With electrophiles, benzene usually undergoes:
blocks.explanation: Unlike alkenes, benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution and not electrophilic addition (20.3).

book_ref.quote: Unlike alkenes, it undergoes the electrophilic substitution and not electrophilic addition reactions

blocks.prompt: 57 Electrophilic addition to benzene is not favourable because it:

options.text: would permanently break the delocalisation of the ring

blocks.explanation: In addition the delocalisation is broken; in substitution it is restored at the end, so the ring keeps its stability (20.3).

book_ref.quote: In electrophilic addition the delocalisation is broken and addition is not favourable.

blocks.prompt: 58 When benzene reacts with bromine in electrophilic substitution, a bromine atom:

options.text: replaces a hydrogen atom of the ring
joins the ring as a seventh atom

blocks.explanation: In electrophilic substitution, bromine replaces a hydrogen atom, keeping the aromatic ring intact (20.3).

book_ref.quote: Bromine in the electrophilic substitution reaction replaces a hydrogen atom.

blocks.prompt: 59 Which compound adds bromine readily without a halogen carrier?
blocks.explanation: Cyclohexene adds bromine readily (electrophilic addition); benzene does not undergo this addition (20.3, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: but cyclohexene adds bromine readily

blocks.prompt: 60 Benzene resembles alkenes in that it:

options.text: undergoes free radical substitution in UV light
is non-polar with σ bonds only
readily adds bromine at room temperature

blocks.explanation: Benzene has three π bonds and, like alkenes, is reactive towards electrophilic species, but it substitutes rather than adds (20.3).

book_ref.quote: Benzene has three π bonds and, as expected, shows some similarities to alkenes

blocks.prompt: 61 The general mechanism of electrophilic aromatic substitution has how many main steps?
blocks.explanation: The steps are: generation of the electrophile, electrophilic attack, restoration of aromaticity (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: the electrophilic aromatic substitution mechanism can be divided into three main steps

blocks.prompt: 62 In electrophilic aromatic substitution the electrophile can be:

options.text: a positive ion or the positive end of a polar molecule

blocks.explanation: The electrophile can be a positive ion or the positive end of a polar molecule (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: The electrophile can be a positive ion or the positive end of a polar molecule.

blocks.prompt: 63 The electrophile in these reactions is usually:

options.text: added directly as a pure substance
produced in situ from suitable reagents

blocks.explanation: Electrophiles usually cannot simply be added; they are produced in situ by adding appropriate reagents (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: The electrophile is produced in situ, by adding appropriate reagents to the reaction mixture.

blocks.prompt: 64 The intermediate formed when the π electrons of benzene attack the electrophile is called:
blocks.explanation: A new σ bond forms between a ring carbon and the electrophile, so the intermediate is called a sigma complex (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: Because of the new sigma bond formed, this intermediate is called a sigma complex.

blocks.prompt: 65 In the sigma complex, the number of π electrons left in the ring is:
blocks.explanation: Aromaticity is disrupted: only four π electrons remain, with the positive charge spread over five carbon atoms (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: there are now only four π electrons and there is a positive charge spread over the five carbon atoms

blocks.prompt: 66 In the sigma complex, the ring carbon carrying both H and the electrophile is:
blocks.explanation: The carbon bonded to the electrophile and H is sp³; its H is removed by the counterion/conjugate base in step 3 (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: the hydrogen on the sp³-hybridized carbon is removed by a counterion/conjugate base

blocks.prompt: 67 Aromaticity is restored in the last step by:

options.text: homolytic cleavage of the C–C bond
heterolytic cleavage of the C–H bond

blocks.explanation: The H is removed by heterolytic cleavage of the C–H bond; its electrons return to the π system (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: This happens by heterolytic cleavage of the C-H bond.

blocks.prompt: 68 Benzene undergoes substitution with bromine or chlorine only in the presence of:
blocks.explanation: Benzene only reacts with bromine and chlorine (substitution) in the presence of Lewis acids, which generate strong electrophiles (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: Benzene only reacts with bromine and chlorine in the presence of Lewis acids

blocks.prompt: 69 Which of the following is NOT one of the Lewis acids named for halogenation of benzene?
blocks.explanation: The Lewis acids used are usually AlCl₃, FeCl₃ or FeBr₃ (20.3.1). NaCl is not a Lewis acid catalyst here.

book_ref.quote: The Lewis acids are usually aluminum chloride (AlCl₃), iron chloride (FeCl₃) or iron bromide (FeBr₃).

blocks.prompt: 70 In the bromination of benzene with Br₂ and AlBr₃, the electrophile is:
blocks.explanation: AlBr₃ polarises Br₂ and generates the electrophile Br⁺, which then follows the general mechanism (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: Once the electrophile is formed, it follows the same general mechanism as we have discussed earlier.

blocks.prompt: 71 In bromination with AlBr₃, the proton is removed from the sigma complex by:
blocks.explanation: In bromination the sigma complex is deprotonated by [AlBr₄]⁻, giving HBr and regenerating AlBr₃ (20.3.1, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: In bromination the sigma complex is deprotonated by [AlBr₄]⁻

blocks.prompt: 72 When Br₂ is polarised by the Lewis acid, its partial charges are written as:
blocks.explanation: Partial charges are δ+ and δ− (20.3.1, Book correction to the printed σ+/σ−).

book_ref.quote: partial charges are δ+ and δ−

blocks.prompt: 73 In the chlorination of benzene, the electrophile Cl⁺ is generated using:
blocks.explanation: FeCl₃ is used as the Lewis acid activator for generating Cl⁺; the rest of the mechanism is as for bromination (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: FeCl₃ is used as the Lewis acid activator for generating Cl⁺

blocks.prompt: 74 The nitrating mixture used to introduce a nitro group on benzene is:
blocks.explanation: Nitro group is introduced using a mixture of conc. HNO₃ and conc. H₂SO₄ (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: using mixture of conc. HNO₃ and conc. H₂SO₄

blocks.prompt: 75 The electrophile in the nitration of benzene is:
blocks.explanation: The electrophile NO₂⁺ (nitronium ion) is generated by reacting conc. HNO₃ with conc. H₂SO₄ (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: The electrophile NO₂⁺ ion is generated by reacting concentrated nitric acid

blocks.prompt: 76 If benzene is nitrated at a higher temperature:

options.text: more than one nitro group is likely to be substituted

blocks.explanation: At higher temperatures there is a greater chance of more than one nitro group being substituted (20.3.1, Mechanism).

book_ref.quote: At higher temperatures there is a greater chance of getting more than one nitro group substituted onto the ring.

blocks.prompt: 77 The dinitro product formed in small amount even at 50 °C during nitration of benzene is:
blocks.explanation: A certain amount of 1,3-dinitrobenzene forms even at 50 °C; –NO₂ is a meta director (20.3.1, 20.4).

book_ref.quote: You will get a certain amount of 1,3-dinitrobenzene formed even at 50°C.

blocks.prompt: 78 Friedel-Crafts alkylation introduces into the benzene ring:
blocks.explanation: In Friedel-Crafts alkylation an alkyl group is substituted into the benzene ring (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: In the Friedel-Crafts alkylation, an alkyl group is substituted into the benzene ring.

blocks.prompt: 79 An acyl group is:

options.text: an alkyl group attached to oxygen, R–O–
an alkyl group attached to nitrogen
a benzene ring attached to a carbonyl group only
an alkyl group attached to a carbonyl group, R–C=O

blocks.explanation: An acyl group is an alkyl group attached to a carbonyl group, R–C=O (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: An acyl group is an alkyl group attached to a carbonyl group, R-C=O.

blocks.prompt: 80 In Friedel-Crafts alkylation, the electrophile formed from the alkyl halide and AlCl₃ is:
blocks.explanation: AlCl₃ reacts with the alkyl halide to form a carbocation, which acts as the electrophile (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: resulting in the formation of a carbocation which acts as an electrophile

blocks.prompt: 81 In Friedel-Crafts acylation, the electrophile is:
blocks.explanation: AlCl₃ forms a complex with the acyl halide, which loses a halide ion forming the acylium ion RCO⁺ (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: the acyl halide loses a halide ion, forming an acylium ion

blocks.prompt: 82 In Friedel-Crafts alkylation, the AlCl₃ catalyst is regenerated when:

options.text: the alkyl halide is formed again
the proton lost from the intermediate forms HCl

blocks.explanation: Deprotonation of the arenium ion restores aromaticity; this proton forms HCl, regenerating AlCl₃ (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: This proton goes on to form hydrochloric acid, regenerating the AlCl₃ catalyst.

blocks.prompt: 83 When the benzene ring attacks the carbocation in Friedel-Crafts alkylation, the arenium ion intermediate:
blocks.explanation: The π electrons attack the carbocation forming an arenium ion; aromaticity is temporarily lost and restored on deprotonation (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: The aromaticity of the arene is temporarily lost

blocks.prompt: 84 Benzene reacts with chloroethane (CH₃CH₂Cl) in the presence of AlCl₃. The organic product is:
blocks.explanation: This is Friedel-Crafts alkylation: the ethyl carbocation substitutes into the ring, giving C₆H₅CH₂CH₃ and HCl (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: In the Friedel-Crafts acylation reaction, an acyl group is substituted into the benzene ring

blocks.prompt: 85 The product of Friedel-Crafts acylation of benzene with an acyl chloride RCOCl is:
blocks.explanation: Friedel-Crafts acylation gives the acyl benzene C₆H₅COR; the proton lost forms HCl and AlCl₃ is regenerated (20.3.1).

book_ref.quote: Thus, the required acyl benzene product is obtained via the Friedel-Crafts acylation reaction.

blocks.prompt: 86 The position taken by a second incoming electrophile on a substituted benzene is decided by:

options.text: the size of the reaction vessel
the group already attached to the ring

blocks.explanation: Any group attached to the benzene ring affects electrophilic substitution and determines the orientation (20.4).

book_ref.quote: determines the orientation of the substitution

blocks.prompt: 87 Meta-directing groups are mostly:

options.text: electron-withdrawing groups that destabilize the arenium ion
electron-donating groups that stabilize the arenium ion
groups with no effect on reactivity

blocks.explanation: Meta directors are mostly electron-withdrawing; they destabilize the arenium intermediate and deactivate the ring (20.4).

book_ref.quote: Such groups are mostly electron-withdrawing groups, that destabilize the arenium intermediate.

blocks.prompt: 88 A meta-directing group makes the benzene ring:
blocks.explanation: A meta director makes the ring less reactive than benzene and sends the electrophile to the meta position (20.4).

book_ref.quote: Group that makes the ring less reactive than benzene

blocks.prompt: 89 Which of the following is a meta-directing group?
blocks.explanation: Examples of meta directors: –CN, C=O, –NO₂, –CO₂– (20.4). –OH, –NR₂ and –R are ortho-para directors.

book_ref.quote: include -CN, C=O, -NO₂, -CO₂-

blocks.prompt: 90 The major product of chlorination of nitrobenzene is:
blocks.explanation: –NO₂ is a meta director, so chlorination of nitrobenzene occurs at the meta position (1,3) (20.4).

book_ref.quote: its chlorination occurs at the meta position

blocks.prompt: 91 Which of the following is an ortho-para directing group?
blocks.explanation: Ortho-para directors: –SR, –R, –OH, –OR, –NR₂, –SH (20.4); –CN, –NO₂ and C=O are meta directors.

book_ref.quote: are -SR, -R, -OH, -OR, -NR₂, -SH

blocks.prompt: 92 Ortho-para directing groups have the ability to:

options.text: donate electrons to the benzene ring

blocks.explanation: Ortho-para directors are groups able to donate electrons to the benzene ring; they activate it (20.4).

book_ref.quote: Note that these are groups that have the ability to donate electrons to the benzene ring.

blocks.prompt: 93 With an ortho-para director on the ring, the meta product is:
blocks.explanation: With ortho-para directors, ortho and para products dominate (slight preference for para); meta is an extremely minor byproduct (20.4).

book_ref.quote: and the meta- product is an extremely minor byproduct

blocks.prompt: 94 Between the ortho and para products of an ortho-para director, there is a slight preference for:

options.text: neither, they are always exactly equal

blocks.explanation: Ortho-para directors give either the ortho (1,2) or para (1,4) product, with a slight preference for para (20.4).

book_ref.quote: A group that makes the ring more reactive than benzene

blocks.prompt: 95 Ring chlorination of methylbenzene gives a mixture of:
blocks.explanation: The methyl group is 2,4-directing, so chlorine gives 2-chloromethylbenzene and 4-chloromethylbenzene (20.4).

book_ref.quote: a mixture of 2-chloromethylbenzene and 4-chloromethylbenzene

blocks.prompt: 96 The conditions for chlorinating the ring of methylbenzene are:

options.text: AlCl₃ or iron, no UV light, room temperature

blocks.explanation: Ring chlorination of methylbenzene uses AlCl₃ (or iron) in the absence of UV light at room temperature (20.4).

book_ref.quote: The reactions take place at room temperature.

blocks.prompt: 97 In phenol, incoming electrophiles tend to go to positions:
blocks.explanation: The OH group is a ring activator; incoming groups go into the 2, 4 and 6 positions (20.4).

book_ref.quote: OH group is also ring activator so incoming groups will tend to go into the 2, 4 & 6 positions on the ring

blocks.prompt: 98 Two molecules of methylbenzene are chlorinated, one giving the 2-chloro and the other the 4-chloro isomer. The number of HCl molecules formed is:
blocks.explanation: Each substitution replaces one H with Cl and releases one HCl: 2C₆H₅CH₃ + 2Cl₂ → isomers + 2HCl (20.4, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: it is drawn with 2 methylbenzene + 2Cl2

blocks.prompt: 99 When benzene burns in excess air, the products are:
blocks.explanation: In excess air benzene is completely oxidized to CO₂ and H₂O: 2C₆H₆ + 15O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O (20.4.1).

book_ref.quote: When benzene is burnt in excess of air, it is completely oxidized to CO₂ and H₂O.

blocks.prompt: 100 Burning benzene gives a smoky flame. This is used as:
blocks.explanation: The combustion of benzene gives a smoky flame, used as a test for aromatic compounds (20.4.1).

book_ref.quote: this reaction gives a smoky flame which is used as a test for aromatic compounds

blocks.prompt: 101 From 2C₆H₆ + 15O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O, the moles of O₂ needed to burn 1 mol of benzene completely are:
blocks.explanation: 2 mol C₆H₆ need 15 mol O₂, so 1 mol needs 15/2 = 7.5 mol O₂ (20.4.1).

book_ref.quote: However, this reaction gives a smoky flame

blocks.prompt: 102 Using 2C₆H₆ + 15O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O, the moles of CO₂ formed from 0.25 mol of benzene are:
blocks.explanation: 12 mol CO₂ per 2 mol C₆H₆ = 6 mol per mol; 0.25 × 6 = 1.5 mol CO₂ (20.4.1).

book_ref.quote: it is completely oxidized to CO₂ and H₂O

blocks.prompt: 103 Side-chain oxidation takes place at:

options.text: the carbon atoms of the ring
a hydrogen atom of the ring
the π cloud of benzene only
an alkyl group directly attached to the benzene ring

blocks.explanation: Oxidation at an alkyl group directly attached to a benzene ring is side-chain oxidation; the ring stays intact (20.4.2).

book_ref.quote: Oxidation reaction that takes place at an alkyl group directly attached to a benzene ring is termed as side-chain oxidation.

blocks.prompt: 104 Which reagent is NOT listed for side-chain oxidation of alkylbenzenes?
blocks.explanation: Alkylbenzenes are oxidized by alkaline KMnO₄, acidic K₂Cr₂O₇ or dilute HNO₃ (20.4.2); H₂/Ni is used for hydrogenation, a reduction.

book_ref.quote: alkylbenzenes are readily oxidized by alkaline KMnO₄ or acidic K₂Cr₂O₇ or dilute HNO₃

blocks.prompt: 105 Side-chain oxidation of methylbenzene (toluene) gives:
blocks.explanation: The alkyl group is oxidized to a carboxylic acid group, keeping the ring intact: toluene gives benzoic acid (20.4.2).

book_ref.quote: regardless of the size of alkyl group, keeping the benzene ring intact

blocks.prompt: 106 Ethylbenzene, C₆H₅CH₂CH₃, on side-chain oxidation with KMnO₄ gives:
blocks.explanation: Whatever the length of the alkyl group, it gives only one carboxyl group attached to the ring: benzoic acid (20.4.2).

book_ref.quote: it gives only on carboxyl group as a product after oxidation

blocks.prompt: 107 Which alkylbenzene does NOT undergo side-chain oxidation with KMnO₄?
blocks.explanation: Oxidation needs at least one benzylic hydrogen; a tertiary carbon attached to the ring has none, so no reaction (20.4.2).

book_ref.quote: No reaction occurs in the absence of benzylic hydrogen.

blocks.prompt: 108 Side-chain oxidation of an alkylbenzene takes place only when the benzylic carbon carries:
blocks.explanation: Side-chain oxidation takes place when there is at least one benzylic hydrogen attached to that carbon (20.4.2).

book_ref.quote: when there is at least one benzylic hydrogen attached to the carbon

blocks.prompt: 109 Although alkanes and benzene both resist oxidation, alkylbenzenes are oxidized because:

options.text: the benzylic carbon attached to the ring becomes more reactive
the ring carbon atoms become sp³
the π electrons leave the ring

blocks.explanation: When put together, the benzylic carbon directly attached to the ring becomes more reactive and susceptible to oxidation (20.4.2).

book_ref.quote: the benzylic carbon which is directly attached to the benzene ring becomes more reactive

blocks.prompt: 110 In the KMnO₄ test, an alkylbenzene with benzylic hydrogen:

options.text: discharges the purple colour of KMnO₄

blocks.explanation: The purple colour of KMnO₄ is discharged as it is consumed in oxidizing the alkylbenzene (20.4.2).

book_ref.quote: Purple colour of KMnO₄ solution is discharged

blocks.prompt: 111 Besides alkaline KMnO₄, alkylbenzenes are readily oxidised by:
blocks.explanation: Alkylbenzenes are readily oxidised by alkaline KMnO₄, acidic K₂Cr₂O₇ or dilute HNO₃ (20.4.2).

book_ref.quote: alkylbenzenes are readily oxidized by alkaline KMnO₄ or acidic K₂Cr₂O₇ or dilute HNO₃

blocks.prompt: 112 An arene carries a methyl, an isopropyl and an isobutyl group at positions 1, 3 and 5; each has benzylic hydrogen. Complete side-chain oxidation gives:
blocks.explanation: Every alkyl group with a benzylic hydrogen becomes one –COOH, whatever its length: benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylic acid (20.4.2, 20.4.3 Quick Check).

book_ref.quote: The answer to the question is the same: benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylic acid.

blocks.prompt: 113 Complete hydrogenation of benzene gives:
blocks.explanation: Cyclohexane is produced when benzene is completely hydrogenated (20.4.3).

book_ref.quote: Cyclohexane is produced when benzene is completely hydrogenated.

blocks.prompt: 114 The number of moles of H₂ needed to convert 1 mol of benzene completely into cyclohexane is:
blocks.explanation: Hydrogenation adds 1, 2 or 3 mol H₂; complete hydrogenation to cyclohexane (C₆H₁₂) needs 3 mol (20.4.3).

book_ref.quote: involves the addition of 1, 2, or 3 moles of hydrogen to the carbons of benzene

blocks.prompt: 115 Hydrogenation of benzene is carried out using:

options.text: finely divided nickel, about 150 °C, higher pressure

blocks.explanation: The same finely divided nickel catalyst as for alkenes is used at similar temperatures (around 150 °C) but at higher pressure (20.4.3).

book_ref.quote: the same finely divided nickel catalyst that is used in hydrogenation of alkenes

blocks.prompt: 116 Although hydrogenation of benzene is exothermic overall, it needs harsher conditions because:

options.text: there is a high activation barrier

blocks.explanation: The reaction is exothermic overall due to strong new C–H bonds, but has a high activation barrier, so higher pressure is applied (20.4.3).

book_ref.quote: there is a high activation barrier to the reaction

blocks.prompt: 117 Addition reactions of benzene:

options.text: destroy the electron delocalisation of the ring
increase the number of π electrons
replace hydrogen atoms of the ring

blocks.explanation: Addition destroys the delocalisation because those electrons form bonds with the new atoms (20.4.3).

book_ref.quote: These reactions destroy the electron delocalisation in the original benzene ring

blocks.prompt: 118 Complete addition of chlorine to benzene takes place in the presence of:

options.text: UV light and heat, without a catalyst

blocks.explanation: In the absence of a catalyst, UV light and heat are sufficient for complete halogenation (addition) of benzene (20.4.3).

book_ref.quote: In the absence of a catalyst, UV light and heat are sufficient for complete halogenation.

blocks.prompt: 119 The molecular formula of the product of complete addition of chlorine to benzene is:
blocks.explanation: Three Cl₂ molecules add across the ring: C₆H₆ + 3Cl₂ → C₆H₆Cl₆; no hydrogen is lost in addition (20.4.3).

book_ref.quote: The complete chlorination of benzene is shown below:

blocks.prompt: 120 Taking C = 12, H = 1 and Cl = 35.5 g mol⁻¹, the molar mass of the complete chlorine addition product of benzene, C₆H₆Cl₆, is:

book_ref.quote: Chlorine and bromine react in the same way.

blocks.prompt: 121 Complete hydrogenation of methylbenzene gives:
blocks.explanation: Methylbenzene adds 3H₂ to give methylcyclohexane (20.4.3).

book_ref.quote: involves the addition of 1, 2, or 3 moles of hydrogen to the carbons of benzene

blocks.prompt: 122 Cyclohexane, made by hydrogenation of benzene, is useful as:

options.text: a solvent and a precursor for other chemicals

blocks.explanation: Cyclohexane is a useful solvent and a precursor in the production of other chemicals (20.4.3).

book_ref.quote: Cyclohexane is a useful solvent and a precursor in the production of other chemicals.
